rv.q: What's inevitably lost is the excitement of watching a single performer act the chameleon, flipping between characters as if changing psychic TV channels. But what's gained in the new staging, directed by Whitney White, is the warm camaraderie of an ensemble work.
Five top-tier talents in one evening... The Whoopi Monologues have been reborn for a new generation and are not showing their age.
This sterling revival demonstrates that, with the right actors and creative talent, The Whoopi Monologues is strong enough to make an impact without its namesake star.
Young (Purlie Victorious, Purpose) is flawless, whether discussing the Anne Frank house in Amsterdam, eyes full of wonder, or describing the airplane meal.
Lewis gives us a master class in a performance that soars.
Read our review of The Whoopi Monologues off Broadway, a reimagined version of Whoopi Goldberg's self-titled 1984 solo show now directed by Whitney White.
The evening ultimately feels like less than the sum of its parts.

Kecia Lewis (Hell’s Kitchen) charges through the evolution of women’s sanitary health products and offers an extended riff on menopause that mostly succeeds (the actress called for her next line several times at my performance). Many of the routines take a turn toward sentimentality or pathos toward the end — with mixed results.

cn.t: Critics praise this revival of Whoopi Goldberg's 1984 solo show, now performed by five talented actresses who deliver stellar performances. The production successfully highlights Goldberg's gifts as a writer and social observer.
